Use the smooth off-shell coordinate model $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$, with $x^0=c_{\mathrm{light}}t$ in SI coordinates, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, increasing $x^0$ as the future direction, and standard orientation. The scalar time-ordering convention sets $c_{\mathrm{light}}=1$, so $x^0$ is the length coordinate in that convention as well. Here off shell means that no field equation is imposed. Take smooth real components $a_\mu\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$ and a smooth commuting matter field $\psi\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C^4)$. Use the normalized real potential $a=a_\mu dx^\mu$ and dimensionless coupling $g=q\sqrt{\mu_0c_{\mathrm{light}}/\hbar}$ of the charged-gauge-data convention; $a_\mu$ has units $\mathrm m^{-1}$, $g$ is dimensionless, and $\psi$ has units $\mathrm m^{-3/2}$. The exact supplier convention is $a'_\mu=a_\mu+\partial_\mu\alpha$, $\psi'=e^{ig\alpha}\psi$, for a smooth dimensionless real infinitesimal gauge parameter $\alpha$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be the free graded-commutative $\mathbb C$-algebra over $C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C)$ generated by the finite jets of $a_\mu$, $\psi$, an odd ghost $c_{\mathrm{gh}}$, an odd antighost $\bar c$, and an even auxiliary variable $B$. Every element of $\mathcal P$ is a polynomial in finitely many jet coordinates. The fields $a_\mu$ and $\psi$ have Grassmann parity $0$ and ghost number $0$; $c_{\mathrm{gh}}$ has parity $1$ and ghost number $1$; $\bar c$ has parity $1$ and ghost number $-1$; and $B$ has parity $0$ and ghost number $0$. The ghost and nonminimal variables are formal algebraic generators; no state-space or positivity claim is made. The generators $c_{\mathrm{gh}},\bar c,B$ carry no physical unit assignment, and the differential below is dimensionless. The subscript distinguishes the ghost from the speed of light $c_{\mathrm{light}}$.

Let $s$ vanish on the coefficient algebra, so $s f=0$ for every $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C)$. Thus $s$ is $C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C)$-linear.

Define the odd derivation $s:\mathcal P\to\mathcal P$ of ghost number $1$ by
$$
sa_\mu=\partial_\mu c_{\mathrm{gh}},\qquad sc_{\mathrm{gh}}=0,\qquad s\bar c=B,\qquad sB=0,\qquad s\psi=igc_{\mathrm{gh}}\psi .
$$
Extend $s$ by the graded Leibniz rule $s(XY)=(sX)Y+(-1)^{|X|}X(sY)$ for homogeneous $X$, where $|X|$ is Grassmann parity, and by $s(\partial^\beta X)=\partial^\beta(sX)$ for every multi-index $\beta$. This is an off-shell local algebraic differential for the Abelian gauge transformations; it is not a BRST charge on a Hilbert space and it does not assert existence of a gauge-invariant quantum theory.

derivations.claim: On the gauge and nonminimal generators, $s^2a_\mu=s(\partial_\mu c_{\mathrm{gh}})=\partial_\mu(sc_{\mathrm{gh}})=0$, $s^2c_{\mathrm{gh}}=0$, $s^2\bar c=sB=0$, and $s^2B=0$. Commutation of $s$ with spacetime derivatives gives the same equality on every jet of these generators.

Since $c_{\mathrm{gh}}$ is odd in a graded-commutative algebra over $\mathbb C$, $c_{\mathrm{gh}}^2=-c_{\mathrm{gh}}^2$ and hence $c_{\mathrm{gh}}^2=0$. The graded Leibniz rule therefore gives
$$s^2\psi=s(igc_{\mathrm{gh}}\psi)=-igc_{\mathrm{gh}}(igc_{\mathrm{gh}}\psi)=g^2c_{\mathrm{gh}}^2\psi=0.$$

The square of an odd derivation is an even derivation: the two mixed terms in $s^2(XY)$ cancel by the graded Leibniz rule. It vanishes on every generator and every jet by steps 1.1–1.2, so it vanishes on each finite polynomial in $\mathcal P$.

Now $s^2=0$ by step 2.1, so $s$ is a differential. It preserves the number of the selected doublet variables: its action on the other generators is independent of them, and each term $v^j\partial_L/\partial u^j$ replaces one $u^j$ by one $v^j$. Thus $[N,s]=0$. On each pair, $hu^j=0$, $hv^j=u^j$, $su^j=v^j$, and $sv^j=0$, so $(sh+hs)u^j=u^j$ and $(sh+hs)v^j=v^j$. Both $sh+hs$ and $N$ are even derivations and vanish on the doublet-independent generators; equality on generators proves $sh+hs=N$ on the polynomial algebra.

Let $a_k$ be $s$-closed and homogeneous of doublet number $k>0$. Since $[N,s]=0$, the homogeneous components of any $s$-closed polynomial are separately $s$-closed. Applying $sh+hs=N$ to $a_k$ gives $s(ha_k)=ka_k$ because $sa_k=0$; division by the nonzero integer $k$ yields $a_k=s(ha_k/k)$.

Every polynomial has a finite decomposition $a=\sum_{k\ge0}a_k$. For an $s$-closed $a$, step 4.1 makes every $a_k$ with $k>0$ exact, while $a_0$ is closed by $[N,s]=0$. Therefore every extended cohomology class has a representative in the doublet-independent subalgebra.

If a doublet-independent closed polynomial $a_0$ is $s b$ in the extended algebra, take the doublet-number-zero component $b_0$ of the finite decomposition of $b$. Because $s$ preserves $N$, the number-zero component of $sb=a_0$ is $s b_0=a_0$. Thus a class from the minimal subalgebra becomes exact in the extension only if it was already exact there, proving injectivity as well as the surjectivity in step 5.1.

The degree-zero component is exactly the surviving minimal sector in steps 5.1–6.1.

boundaries.evidence: Surjectivity of the cohomology inclusion is established by the positive-degree contraction in step 5.1.
Injectivity is established by projecting an extended primitive to doublet number zero in step 6.1.

finite_checks.disposition: Direct generator check of step 3.1; both sides are even derivations.

The Abelian jet derivation $s$ defined in the local BRST algebra satisfies $s^2=0$. More generally, take any finite set of jet doublets $u^j,v^j$ with $|v^j|=|u^j|+1\pmod 2$, $\operatorname{gh}(v^j)=\operatorname{gh}(u^j)+1$, $su^j=v^j$, and $sv^j=0$, and suppose the transformations of all other generators are independent of these doublets. Define the doublet-number operator
$$N=\sum_j\left(u^j\frac{\partial_L}{\partial u^j}+v^j\frac{\partial_L}{\partial v^j}\right)$$
and the odd homotopy $h=\sum_j u^j\frac{\partial_L}{\partial v^j}$, using left graded derivatives. Then $[N,s]=0$ and $sh+hs=N$. Consequently the inclusion of the doublet-independent polynomial subalgebra induces an isomorphism on polynomial BRST cohomology. In particular, if $sa_k=0$ and $Na_k=ka_k$ for a positive integer $k$, then $a_k=s(ha_k/k)$.

For a ghost-number grading, write this cohomology as
$$H^r(s,\mathcal P)=\ker(s:\mathcal P^r\to\mathcal P^{r+1})/\operatorname{im}(s:\mathcal P^{r-1}\to\mathcal P^r).$$

Use the four-dimensional coordinate and jet algebra and nilpotent differential $s$ fixed by the earlier Abelian local BRST definition and nilpotence lemma. For integers $r$ and $0\le p\le4$, a compactly supported local horizontal $p$-form of ghost number $r$ is a finite sum of terms
$$f_{i_1\ldots i_p}(x,z)\,dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_p},$$
where each coefficient is smooth and compactly supported in $x\in\mathbb R^4$, polynomial in finitely many field-jet coordinates $z$, and homogeneous of ghost number $r$. Denote this space by $\Omega^{r,p}_{\mathrm{loc},c}$. A left derivative is used for odd jet coordinates.

For each spacetime index $\mu$, define the total derivative on a local coefficient by
$$D_\mu=\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\mu}+\sum_{i,\alpha}z^i_{\alpha+e_\mu}\frac{\partial_L}{\partial z^i_\alpha},$$
where $\alpha$ ranges over multi-indices, $i$ over the field and ghost generators, and $e_\mu$ is the multi-index with one derivative in direction $\mu$. The horizontal exterior derivative is $d_H=dx^\mu\wedge D_\mu$. It satisfies $d_H^2=0$. Extend $s$ to a homogeneous $p$-form by $s\omega=(-1)^p s_{\mathrm{coeff}}\omega$, where $s_{\mathrm{coeff}}$ acts on its coefficient by the earlier local BRST definition; then $s^2=0$ and $s d_H+d_Hs=0$.

Set $\Omega^{r,p}_{\mathrm{loc},c}=0$ for $p<0$ or $p>4$. Evaluation of a compactly supported local four-form on any smooth off-shell configuration is a finite integral.

For a graded subcomplex $\mathcal K^{r,p}\subseteq\Omega^{r,p}_{\mathrm{loc},c}$ stable under $s$ and $d_H$, define
$$Z^{r,p}(s|d_H;\mathcal K)=\{a_p\in\mathcal K^{r,p}:\ s a_p+d_Ha_{p-1}=0\text{ for some }a_{p-1}\in\mathcal K^{r+1,p-1}\}$$
and
$$B^{r,p}(s|d_H;\mathcal K)=\{s b_p+d_Hc_{p-1}:\ b_p\in\mathcal K^{r-1,p},\ c_{p-1}\in\mathcal K^{r,p-1}\}.$$
The relative local BRST cohomology is $H^{r,p}(s|d_H;\mathcal K)=Z^{r,p}/B^{r,p}$. In four dimensions, $H^1(s|d_H)$ is shorthand for $H^{1,4}(s|d_H)$. For compactly supported coefficients, $\int_{\mathbb R^4}d_Hc_3=0$ by the one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus in each coordinate and Fubini's theorem, so the quotient by $d_H$ identifies densities that define the same integrated local functional.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix any admissible flat scalar free datum and local scalar polynomial class as defined by the local time-ordered product contract. Then there exists a sequence of symmetric multilinear maps $T_n$ satisfying that contract at every finite perturbative order. At order $n$, each numerical graph distribution has a finite upper scaling bound in the $4(n-1)$ relative coordinates. At the analytic extension stage, independent balanced coefficients admit extensions preserving their actual scaling degree; total-derivative labels and the final local normalizations obey the engineering scaling upper bounds prescribed by the contract. For a fixed punctured coefficient with bound $B_\Gamma$, the extension ambiguity is contained in the finite span of derivatives of the diagonal delta distribution of order at most $\lfloor B_\Gamma-4(n-1)\rfloor$ when $B_\Gamma\ge4(n-1)$, and is zero when $B_\Gamma<4(n-1)$, subject also to the linearity and derivative identities. For the analytic degree-preserving extension family of an independent balanced coefficient, one can use its actual degree in place of $B_\Gamma$. Thus the coefficients form a formal series only; no convergence in the coupling, adiabatic limit, positivity claim, or gauge/Ward identity is asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Under the hypotheses of [F3], including [A3] and [A4], the scalar time-ordering input exists as a formal coefficientwise scheme. Fix such a scheme as background. The additional operator $\mathcal W_\hbar$, its nilpotence, and the locality premise in [A1]–[A2] are separate hypotheses not supplied by [F3].

Apply $\mathcal W_\hbar$ to the expansion in [A1]. Since $\mathcal W_\hbar^2X=0$, its order-$\hbar^n$ coefficient is the leading operator $s$ applied to $\mathcal A$; all terms from the positive powers of $\hbar$ in $\mathcal W_\hbar$ have order at least $n+1$. Hence $s\mathcal A=0$ in $\mathscr F_n^2$.

Since $\mathcal A=[a_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$ and $s\mathcal A=0$ in $\mathscr F_n^2$, the quotient definition in [F2] gives $s a_4=d_Hc_3$ for some $c_3\in\mathcal K_n^{2,3}$, after absorbing a sign into $c_3$. Thus $a_4$ is a cocycle in the specified relative local cohomology.

If $[a_4]_{s|d_H}=0$, the quotient definition in [F2], restricted to $\mathcal K_n$, supplies $b_4\in\mathcal K_n^{0,4}$ and $c_3\in\mathcal K_n^{1,3}$ such that $a_4=s b_4+d_Hc_3$. This uses the cocycle conclusion of step 3.1 so the relative class is defined.

The counterterm class $[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$ is admissible by [A2]. Replacing $X$ by $X-\hbar^n[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$ changes the order-$n$ breaking by $-s[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$, because the leading term of $\mathcal W_\hbar$ is $s$. Step 4.1 gives $[a_4]_{\mathscr F_n}=s[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$, since $d_Hc_3$ is zero in that quotient, so the breaking is canceled.

Conversely, if an admissible local counterterm class $[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$ cancels the order-$n$ breaking in $\mathscr F_n^1$, then $[a_4]_{\mathscr F_n}-s[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}=0$. By the quotient definition in [F2], $a_4-sb_4=d_Hc_3$ for some $c_3\in\mathcal K_n^{1,3}$. This is exactly the relative coboundary condition; step 3.1 ensures that $[a_4]_{s|d_H}$ is the class under discussion.

The coefficient argument applies at n=1: every positive-hbar term on hbar^n A has order at least n+1, as in step 2.1.
A density that is d_H-exact in K_n represents zero in F_n; steps 4.1–5.1 verify its removal by the zero counterterm.

If the relative class vanishes, steps 4.1–5.1 construct an admissible counterterm that cancels the order-n coefficient.
If a counterterm cancels in F_n, step 6.1 gives the required K_n-relative coboundary.

For a_4=s b_4+d_H c_3, the shift X-hbar^n[b_4] changes the order-n class by -s[b_4], leaving [d_H c_3]=0 in F_n.
finite_checks.disposition: Sign and same-complex quotient check of step 5.1.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked all six proof steps and all five exact mathematical suppliers. Stable same-subcomplex quotient makes induced s well-defined; s-squared=0 and sd_H=-d_Hs imply relative coboundaries are cocycles. Extracting order n from W_hbar-squared X gives sA=0 because n>=1 and all other contributions have degree >=n+1. Kernel of the quotient map gives the K_n^{2,3} primitive. Class zero supplies an admissible K_n^{0,4} counterterm and K_n^{1,3} remainder; shift by minus hbar^n[b] cancels exactly its leading s[b]. Conversely cancellation gives a relative coboundary in the same complex. Existence is essential: an arbitrary b need not cancel. derivations.claim: Since $B$ is even, the graded Leibniz rule gives $s(B^2)=(sB)B+B(sB)=0$, so $B^2$ is $s$-closed.
Because $\bar c$ is odd, $s(\bar c B)=(s\bar c)B-\bar c(sB)=B^2$. Thus $B^2$ is exact with primitive $\bar c B$, whose ghost number is $-1$.

The operator $N$ counts the two factors of $B$, so $N(B^2)=2B^2$, while $hB^2=2\bar c B$. Therefore $s(hB^2/2)=B^2$, agreeing with the general contraction of [F2]. This is an algebraic polynomial identity and makes no statement about a positive norm or a state space.
